prompt: What happened to the Billing team's throughput after the limit, comparing June and July with September?

choices.text: It fell by about a quarter, as the objection predicts
choices.why: That is the worry; the data say otherwise.

choices.text: It rose a little
choices.why: Right. From 6.0 to 7.0 items a week, with work in progress at a quarter.

choices.text: It fell to a quarter, along with work in progress
choices.why: Work in progress fell to a quarter; throughput did not follow it.

choices.text: It cannot be compared, because the periods differ in length
choices.why: Per-week throughput makes periods of any length comparable.

prompt: Before the limit the median cycle time was 18 days; in September it was 4. By what percentage did it fall, to the nearest whole number?
Which two effects in billing.py explain why throughput could rise with less work open?

choices.text: Developers worked longer days and skipped reviews
choices.why: Nobody worked longer, and reviews happened first, not never.

choices.text: Items got smaller and estimates got better
choices.why: Item sizes come from the same distribution throughout.

choices.text: Fewer requests arrived and more people joined
choices.why: Arrivals and the team are the same before and after.

choices.text: Less switching, and help at the review bottleneck
choices.why: Right. One item each removed switching costs; everybody reviewing emptied the queue.

prompt: Why does the lesson say to compare policies by cycle time more readily than by throughput?

choices.text: Cycle time moves a lot with work in progress; throughput moves a little and is noisy
choices.why: Right. One month's throughput can swing by itself, as the no-limit September did.

choices.text: Throughput is not recorded by most boards
choices.why: It is the easiest number of all: count the done column.

choices.text: Stakeholders only care about cycle time
choices.why: They care about lead time and throughput as well.

choices.text: Throughput is always the same under any policy
choices.why: It moved from 122 to 128 over four months; small, not zero.

prompt: What does running python3 billing.py 2026-10-01 simulate?

choices.text: The team with a limit from the first of October onwards
choices.why: The history ends on 30 September, so that limit never takes effect.

choices.text: An extra month of history, to October
choices.why: The end date is fixed; the argument is the day the rules change.

choices.text: The old rules for all four months
choices.why: Right. A date after the history means no limit at all.

choices.text: A different random seed
choices.why: The seeds are fixed in the program; the argument is a date.

prompt: Over the four months, the run with the limit from 1 June finished 128 items and the run with no limit finished 122. What is the difference as a percentage of 122, to the nearest whole number?
In the no-limit run, September's throughput is 9.1 items a week, the highest of any column. What does the lesson conclude?

choices.text: That the old rules are faster after all
choices.why: Over four months the same run finished the fewest items.

choices.text: That one month's throughput is noise
choices.why: Right. The review queue happened to drain quickly that month.

choices.text: That the simulation has a bug in September
choices.why: Nothing is wrong; months vary.

choices.text: That limits only help in summer
choices.why: Nothing in the data depends on the season.

prompt: Why can't you compare individual items between two runs of billing.py with different dates?

choices.text: The item ids are random
choices.why: Ids are numbered in order of arrival.

choices.text: Python changes the seed every time the program runs
choices.why: The seed is fixed; the same command gives the same files.

choices.text: Only the first run writes items.csv
choices.why: Every run rewrites both files.

choices.text: Different rules use the same random numbers in a different order
choices.why: Right. Each run is its own plausible history; compare summaries.

prompt: Match each kind of limit to the way it fails when used alone.

pairs.right: queues between people can still grow
the board as a whole can still hold too much
it gives no hint where work is stuck

right_distractors: it stops urgent work from ever starting

prompt: Why would a one-item-per-developer limit alone have left Bia's review queue where it was?

choices.text: Developers would have waited instead of reviewing
choices.why: Right. The review-first rule is what turned idle time into review time.

choices.text: Because limits per person never work on any team
choices.why: They remove switching costs; they just say nothing about queues.

choices.text: Because Bia would have started more items herself
choices.why: Bia held no items of her own in the simulation.

choices.text: Because the limit would have been set too high to matter
choices.why: One item each is a tight limit; the problem is what people do when they reach it.

prompt: What should a team do with a blocked item under a work-in-progress limit?

choices.text: Move it to a separate list so the limit frees a place
choices.why: That is the door BIL-189 went through.

choices.text: Delete it and recreate it when it is unblocked
choices.why: That resets its age and unbalances the books.

choices.text: Keep it counting, so unblocking it becomes everybody's problem
choices.why: Right. The pressure to unblock it is the point of the limit.

choices.text: Raise the limit by one for each blocked item
choices.why: That is the same door with a formula on it.

prompt: The Billing team's work in progress sat exactly at its limit every day of September. What does that say about the limit?

choices.text: It is too high and should be lowered
choices.why: A limit too high would rarely be reached.

choices.text: Nothing yet; check how old its items are
choices.why: Right. Full with young items is healthy; full with an old item, as here, means something is stuck.

choices.text: It is too low, because the team is always at it
choices.why: A limit is supposed to be reached; that is how it holds the team to finishing.

choices.text: It has stopped working and should be removed
choices.why: September is the month the limit worked best.

prompt: A lane for work that cannot wait, with its own limit of one, is called an ___ lane.
A developer finishes an item and may not start another. In the lesson's order, what do they check?
items: a test, a tool or the documentation

prompt: What is the difference between pushing and pulling work?

choices.text: Push is for features and pull is for bugs
choices.why: The difference is about when work starts, not its type.

choices.text: In a pull system the manager assigns every item
choices.why: Pull is the opposite of assignment from above.

choices.text: Pull systems need special software
choices.why: Toyota did it with paper cards.

choices.text: Pull starts work only when downstream has room
choices.why: Right. Downstream sets the pace, so no queue forms in front of it.

prompt: What is swarming?

choices.text: Several people on the oldest item
choices.why: Right. It looks inefficient by busyness and is efficient by delivery.

choices.text: Starting many items at once so everyone has work
choices.why: That is the opposite: starting, not finishing.

choices.text: Moving every blocked item to its own column at once
choices.why: Moving items does not finish them.

choices.text: A meeting where the team estimates the backlog
choices.why: That is estimation, lesson 9's subject.

prompt: A stakeholder asks for their item to be started this week, and the board is at its limit. What does the limit make visible?

choices.text: That the team is lazy
choices.why: The team is full; that is what the limit says.

choices.text: That the stakeholder's item is unimportant
choices.why: Importance decides order; the limit decides how much runs at once.

choices.text: Starting it means something else waits
choices.why: Right. The trade happens anyway; the limit makes it a decision somebody sees.

choices.text: That the limit should be raised for important people
choices.why: Raising it for each request removes it.

prompt: "People will be idle." What does the Billing team's history answer?

choices.text: That nobody was ever idle for a moment
choices.why: Some idle-looking time happened; it went into reviews.

choices.text: Throughput rose while open work fell
choices.why: Right. From 6.0 to 7.0 a week, with a quarter of the work open.

choices.text: That idle time does not matter to a business
choices.why: It matters; it simply was not lost, it was spent on the bottleneck.

choices.text: That the team hired a reviewer to fill the gaps
choices.why: The same five people and Bia, throughout.

prompt: "Our items are too different in size for a count to mean anything." What does the lesson answer?

choices.text: Make every item exactly the same size first
choices.why: No team can, and none needs to.

choices.text: Limit story points instead of items
choices.why: Lesson 9 shows points add little over counting.

choices.text: Give large items two places on the board
choices.why: A large item holding one place is what reveals it.

choices.text: A big item holding a place shows up as old
choices.why: Right. That invites the useful question: can it be split?

prompt: What does the lesson call the objection nobody says out loud?

choices.text: Visible waiting makes somebody accountable
choices.why: Right. Spread across open items, waiting was nobody's; a queue is somebody's.

choices.text: That limits are a management fashion
choices.why: That one is said out loud often enough.

choices.text: That limits reduce the number of items finished each month
choices.why: That is the first, spoken objection, and the data answer it.

choices.text: That reviewing is less interesting than writing new code
choices.why: Possibly true, and not the one the lesson names.

prompt: A team sets a review column limit of two. What should happen when a third item is ready for review?

choices.text: It goes into review anyway, since the work is done
choices.why: Then the limit is decoration.

choices.text: Its developer starts a new item while it waits
choices.why: That grows work in progress behind the full column.

choices.text: Somebody reviews one of the two first
choices.why: Right. The full column is a signal to help downstream, not to start upstream.

choices.text: The limit is raised to three for that day
choices.why: A limit raised whenever it is reached is not a limit.

prompt: A team finishes 10 items a week with 30 open. It cuts work in progress to 15 and throughput stays at 10. What is the new average cycle time in weeks?
Which signs say a work-in-progress limit needs attention? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: It is never reached
choices.why: Right. It is not limiting anything.

choices.text: It is always full, with old items behind it
choices.why: Right. Something stuck is holding its places.

choices.text: It is always full, with young items behind it
choices.why: That is the healthy case.

choices.text: The expedite lane is used every day
choices.why: Right. Urgency has become the way past the limit.

prompt: A team adopts a limit on 1 March and on 8 March its 85th-percentile cycle time is higher than in February. What is the most likely reading?

choices.text: The limit has made the team slower
choices.why: A week in, finished items are mostly old ones started before the change.

choices.text: Old items are draining out
choices.why: Right. Like the Billing team's August: judge a new limit after the old queue has gone.

choices.text: The percentile was computed wrongly
choices.why: Nothing points at the arithmetic.

choices.text: The limit should be removed at once
choices.why: Removing it a week in decides on leftovers.
